source.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
source.authors: Tom McGrath; Matthew Rahtz; János Kramár; Vladimir Mikulik; S. Legg

record.tranche_reason: The study directly ablates attention and MLP layers using resample ablation and measures direct and downstream effects.
record.gate_note: The study reports layer-ablation results on Chinchilla 7B. It also discusses prior work on backup heads, but those cited findings are not recorded as results from this study. Individual head mechanisms and other ablation distributions are not tested.
record.test_reason: This is one of the original sources (Hydra effect). It resample-ablates attention and MLP layers in Chinchilla 7B on Counterfact and measures downstream compensation against direct effects. Because it is an original source, no verdict labels are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Missing points: the authors also argue that self-repair does not require dropout, since Chinchilla 7B was trained without it. They also note that compensation below 100% leaves some signal for automated ablation. They frame the work as layer-level and leave head-level analysis to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses resample ablation and compares layer-level unembedding-based direct effects with ablation-based total effects, the method reported here for the original finding.
record.method_sensitivity: Compensation differs with network depth: direct and compensatory effects are well-correlated mainly at intermediate layers; early layers have large total but little direct effect, while very late layers have non-negligible direct effect and fewer downstream layers. The balance between attention-layer and MLP responses also shifts with depth.
record.problems: Evidence is limited to one 7-billion-parameter model and Counterfact factual-recall prompts. The authors describe the illustrative results as anecdotal before the full-dataset analysis; no numerical uncertainty estimates are reported, and resample-ablation patch effects have substantial variance.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results left out. Some per-prompt and per-layer values are shown only in figures without extractable numerical values; aggregate statements and explicit numerical results are retained above.

untested.parts: Individual heads, general text, and multiple model families and sizes are all untested. The study uses layer-level ablation in one model on factual recall.
Overcorrection beyond the original effect is not reported. Per-prompt variability of compensation is shown only in scatter plots and is not quantified.
No backup or copy-suppression heads, LayerNorm rescaling, or anti-erasure neurons are identified.
There is no comparison with zero or mean ablation. Only resample ablation is used.

missing.what: Per-layer correlation between Δunembed and Δablate, and the proportion of prompts with Δunembed > Δablate.
Per-layer variance explained and regression slope between direct and compensatory effects; slope values are not extracted.
Early-layer ablations have large total effects but almost no direct effect.

record.verdict_notes: This is an original source for V1 and V2, so no verdicts are given. All self-repair rows use resample ablation (on-distribution), but no ablation types are contrasted. The study covers a single model and dataset and reports no uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests attention-layer, not individual-head, ablations and uses factual-recall prompts from Counterfact.
The study tests layer-level MLP effects on the maximum-likelihood token, not identified neurons or broader token-distribution effects.
Individual attention heads, general text, multiple model families and sizes, and full-distribution compensation are not tested.
The study reports incomplete average restoration and substantial variance across resample patches; it does not explicitly report overcorrection beyond the original effect.
The study does not test the named backup-head, copy-suppression-head, final-LayerNorm-rescaling, or anti-erasure-neuron mechanisms.
Resample ablation is tested; mean ablation is described but not tested.
The study compares direct and ablation-based importance measures for layer-level effects in its tested factual-recall setting.

rows.subject: Chinchilla 7B
rows.operation_detail: Resample-ablated one attention layer using patches from alternative prompts.

conditions.value: attention layer 18 in Figure 1; examples also describe layer 20 as a downstream responder

rows.measure: Change in downstream attention-layer unembedding impact on the maximum-likelihood token
rows.value: A downstream attention layer substantially increases its impact and partially compensates; the example identifies layer 20.
rows.note: The text characterizes the observed increase as partial compensation.
rows.check: Illustrative examples only; the authors call this evidence 'largely anecdotal'. The state is fine. It also bears on V6, since resample ablation was used.

rows.subject: Chinchilla 7B
rows.operation_detail: Resample-ablated each layer and summed downstream changes in direct effects.
rows.measure: Variance in changes in downstream direct effects explained by compensatory response
rows.note: The authors say the compensatory response explains much of the downstream change, but the response does not fully restore the output.
rows.check: 92% is variance in downstream ΔDE explained by the compensatory response at layer 23, not a restoration fraction, so it does not bear on V4. At layer 23 almost all of the response is in the MLPs, so the row mainly bears on V2.

source_check.correct: 92% variance explained at layer 23 of 32; almost all of the response there occurs in erasure MLPs. For V1 specifically, cannot_determine: this aggregate statistic does not establish later-attention compensation or its restoration fraction. The MLP decomposition bears on V2, and resample compensation bears on V6.
source_check.locator_found: Sections 4.1–4.2; Figure 7(b); final paragraph of Section 4.2.
source_check.problem: The observed state cannot apply uniformly to the linked versions: the layer-23 response is almost entirely MLP erasure reduction, rather than the attention-layer compensation named in V1.

rows.subject: Chinchilla 7B
rows.operation_detail: Resample-ablated layers and compared downstream compensatory effects with direct effects.
rows.measure: Slope of linear regression between direct effect and compensatory response
rows.baseline: A slope of 1 would indicate full compensation
rows.value: Less than one at all layers past layer 13
rows.note: The authors state that the ablations retain a nonzero total effect, though it is much smaller than without the downstream responses.
rows.check: Slope below 1 past layer 13 shows incomplete compensation. That is partial for V1 and V2, but it matches V4's 'partial on average' claim. No overcorrection is shown.

source_check.locator_found: Sections 4.1–4.2; Figure 7(d); paragraph describing incomplete restoration.

rows.subject: Chinchilla 7B
rows.operation_detail: Resample-ablated attention layers and measured changes in MLP unembedding effects.

conditions.value: late layers; at layer 23 almost all of the response occurs in erasure MLPs

rows.measure: Change in MLP effect on the maximum-likelihood-token logit following attention ablation
rows.baseline: MLP effects in the intact network
rows.value: The negative MLP effect is attenuated when attention layers promoting the token are knocked out; at layer 23 almost all of the response occurs in erasure MLPs.
rows.note: The study interprets late MLPs as reducing the maximum-likelihood token's logit, with that reduction weakening after relevant attention ablations.
rows.check: This is exactly what V2 describes: late MLPs downregulate the token and the erasure attenuates after ablation. The state should be observed, not partial. It does not bear on V4.

source_check.locator_found: Section 2.5.2, MLP attenuation paragraph; Section 4.2, Figure 8 discussion; Section 6, Findings.

rows.subject: Chinchilla 7B
rows.operation_detail: Resample-ablated attention layers and measured the combined Hydra and MLP response.

conditions.value: middle layers, where the effects are strongest

rows.measure: Fraction of reduction in token logits restored by downstream responses
rows.baseline: The reduction in token logits caused by ablation
rows.note: The stated restoration combines the Hydra effect and reduced MLP erasure.
rows.check: The ~70% figure combines the Hydra effect and reduced MLP erasure at middle layers. It cannot separate V1 from V2.

rows.subject: Chinchilla 7B
rows.operation_detail: Resample-ablated activations with patches from alternative prompts.

conditions.value: 15 alternative prompts for the ablation procedure

rows.measure: Ablated layer's unembedding impact and variation across patches
rows.value: The ablated layer's impact is approximately zero when averaged across patches; there is substantial variance between patches.
rows.uncertainty: Substantial variance between patches; no numerical uncertainty reported
rows.note: This reports noisy but effective resample ablations, an on-distribution intervention using naturally occurring activations.
rows.check: This is a methodological check that resample ablation zeroes the ablated layer's own direct effect. It does not measure self-repair. Variance across patches is not variance of compensation across prompts (V4).

rows.subject: Chinchilla 7B
rows.operation_detail: Compared unembedding-based direct-effect impact with resample-ablation total-effect impact.
rows.measure: Agreement between direct and total effects on the maximum-likelihood-token logit
rows.baseline: Unembedding-based impact as the direct-effect measure
rows.value: Substantial disagreement and low correlation; unembedding impact exceeds ablation impact for most prompts and layers.
rows.note: The authors attribute the discrepancy to downstream counteracting changes, including self-repair and MLP erasure.
rows.check: No numeric correlation was extracted from Figure 2d.

relation.reason: Reports its own interventions and measurements of attention compensation, MLP erasure attenuation, incomplete restoration and attribution discrepancies.

tranche.reason: Original study establishing the layer-level resample-ablation and unembedding-based direct-versus-total-effect measurements.

source_check.notes: The 92% statistic concerns variance explained, while approximately 70% restoration combines attention compensation and reduced MLP erasure. Statement checks concern this study only; cross-study counts and other studies' results were not independently checked.

statements.correction: Section 4.2: direct and compensatory effects correlate well at intermediate layers; early layers have large total but almost no direct effect; very late layers have only non-negligible direct effect. Section 2.5: unembedding-based and ablation-based importance lack correlation at all but late layers.
statements.problem: Conflates direct-versus-compensatory correlation with direct-versus-total correlation. The intermediate-layer result in Section 4.2 concerns direct and compensatory effects.
